User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — I can walk through this and tell you what’s normally deductible, how the home office is treated, whether itemizing probably makes sense, and which forms you’ll use. I have a few quick clarifying questions at the end because a couple of items (student loan interest timing, who the unreimbursed expenses belong to) change the outcome.

Quick summary of your reported 2024 income
- W-2 (Coastal Manufacturing): $68,200  
- Self-employment (photograph

y): $16,300  
- Interest from Capital One 360: $2,100 (reported on 1099‑INT)  
- Merrill Edge: $420 (likely 1099‑DIV or 1099‑INT)  
Estimated total gross income = $87,020.

What you can generally deduct
- Self-employment (photography) business expenses: Deductible on Schedule C. That includes ordinary and necessary expenses of the photography business (supplies, advertising, equipment, client travel, portions of phone/Internet if used for business, etc.). You listed $1,050 unreimbursed expenses — if those w

ere business expenses for the photography work, report them on Schedule C. If they were unreimbursed employee expenses (for your W‑2 job), those are generally NOT deductible for 2018–2025 under current law.
- Home office: Deductible only if you use the 120 sq ft space regularly and exclusively for your photography business and it is your principal place of business (or used to meet clients there). Two methods:
  - Simplified: $5 × 120 sq ft = $600 (straightforward).
  - Actual/regular method: allocate a bus

iness percentage of home expenses. Your allocation = 120 / 740 ≈ 16.22%. For rent $1,750/month → annual rent $21,000; 16.22% of $21,000 ≈ $3,405 could be part of the home-office deduction (plus a share of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you have them). If you have no other qualifying home expenses beyond rent, the actual method (≈$3,405) will normally yield more than the simplified $600.
  - Use Form 8829 if you use the actual method (it computes allowable business-use-of-home expenses). The deducti

on flows to Schedule C.
- Self-employment tax: You’ll owe self-employment tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self-employment income. You may deduct one-half of the self-employment tax as an adjustment to income on Form 1040 (reported on Schedule 1).
- Student loan interest: If you paid qualified student loan interest in 2024, you can generally deduct up to $2,500 as an above-the-line deduction (reported on Schedule 1 / Form 1040), subject to income limits (phaseout based on modified AGI for single file

rs). You mentioned $5,100 (Nelnet, 2018–2021) — that sounds like payments across prior years; only interest you actually paid during the 2024 tax year can be deducted on your 2024 return. You’ll need Form 1098‑E from your servicer for 2024 interest paid.
- Charitable donations: Your $1,500 cash gift to Salvation Army is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A) and you have the receipt. There is no general above‑the‑line charitable deduction for 2024 (except limited temporary rules in prior years).
- Unre

imbursed employee expenses: Not deductible for most employees under current law (through 2025). If the $1,050 is business expenses for your photography work (self-employed), include on Schedule C instead.

Itemize vs. standard deduction — which is better for you?
- To decide, compare your itemized total (Schedule A) to the standard deduction for a single filer. Based on the items you listed, your likely itemizable items are only $1,500 (charitable). That is well below the standard deduction for a single fil

er, so you will almost certainly be better off taking the standard deduction unless you also have other itemizable amounts you haven’t listed (large mortgage interest, significant property taxes, major unreimbursed medical expenses above the threshold, or much larger charitable gifts).
- Home-office and business expenses do NOT affect the decision to itemize because they are deducted on Schedule C (which reduces AGI), not on Schedule A. So even though the home office lowers your taxable income, it doesn’t c

ount as an itemized deduction.

Practical example (rough, illustrative)
- If you use the actual home-office allocation of rent (~$3,405) plus $1,050 business expenses, your Schedule C net profit might be roughly 16,300 − 3,405 − 1,050 = $11,845. That reduces the portion of your income that’s taxable from self-employment and lowers your overall tax/AGI. You’ll also pay self-employment tax on that net, and you can deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment to income. After those adjustments, the standard dedu

ction will still likely exceed $1,500 of itemized deductions, so standard deduction remains the better choice in this scenario.
(If you want, I can run a more precise draft calculation once you confirm a couple of items below.)

Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (main return).  
- Schedule 1 (adjustments) — student loan interest deduction and the half of SE tax appear here.  
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report photography income ($16,300) and business expenses (home office deductio

n, $1,050 if business-related, other expenses).  
- Schedule SE — to compute self-employment tax and the half-SE-tax deduction.  
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual method for the home-office deduction (computes allowable portion of rent/utilities, etc.). If you use the simplified home office method, you do NOT use Form 8829.  
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (for charitable contribution).  
- 1098‑E — from Nelnet (student loan interest paid in 2024) to support the student loan interest deduction.  
- 1

099‑INT / 1099‑DIV / 1099‑NEC — any forms you receive for interest/dividends and nonemployee compensation (clients might issue 1099‑NEC if > $600 in a year). Even if you don’t receive a 1099, you must still report the income.

Other items you should watch / consider
- Estimated tax payments and withholding: If you end up with significant self‑employment tax or income tax not covered by W‑2 withholding, you may owe estimated taxes (or penalty). Consider adjusting W‑2 withholding or making estimated payments

for 2025 if photography income continues.
- Recordkeeping: keep receipts for business expenses, charity receipts, proofs of rent paid and a diagram of the home-office space (size, exclusive use), and Form 1098‑E for any student loan interest.
- If you have capital gains/losses or sales of investment assets through Merrill Edge, you may need Form 8949/Schedule D — you didn’t mention sales so I’m flagging it just in case.

Questions I need to finalize recommendations / run numbers
1. The $5,100 student loan i

nterest: was that the total you paid during 2024, or is that an aggregate paid in earlier years (2018–2021)? If it’s not interest paid in 2024, only the amount paid in 2024 is deductible (up to $2,500).  
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” expenses related to your photography (self‑employment) or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from your W‑2 job? (Self‑employment = deductible on Schedule C; employee unreimbursed expenses = generally not deductible.)  
3. Do you use the 120 sq ft space exclusi

vely and regularly for the photography business (no personal use) and is it your principal place of business or where you meet clients? (If yes, you qualify for the home-office deduction.)  
4. Do you have utilities, renter’s insurance, or other housing expenses that could be allocated to the home office? (If yes, the actual method becomes even more favorable relative to simplified.)  
5. Do you expect similar photography income in 2025 (so I can advise about estimated taxes)?

If you confirm those items I’

ll:
- run a quick numeric example using both the simplified and actual home-office methods and show estimated income tax + self‑employment tax and whether standard deduction or itemizing is better, and  
- give a short step‑by‑step checklist of what to file/attach and what records to keep.

I’m not a CPA — for complex situations or if you want professional representation, I can recommend you consult a tax professional. Would you like me to run the numeric example now? If so, please answer those 5 quick clar
ifying questions.
